newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada foreign currency rating won't rise soon-S&P.
newsitem.headline: Canada foreign currency rating won't rise soon-S&P.

text.p: Standard & Poor's is unlikely to upgrade Canada's foreign currency credit rating in the near future although the country's financial situtation has improved, an S&P official said on Monday.
But the agency is considering changing the outlook on the rating to stable from negative if it sees evidence the government is committed to improving its finances further.
"At Standard & Poor's we think the champagne should be kept in the ice bucket for a little while yet," Tom Connell, director of Canadian ratings for the agency, told a conference call.
Connell said that while Canada had made great strides in lowering its deficit, there were a number of factors that made an upgrade of its foreign currency debt rating unlikely at this time.

The New York-based rating agency currently assigns a rating of AA+ with a negative outlook to Canada's foreign currency debt. The agency lowered Canada's foreign currency debt rating from AAA in 1992 and revised the debt rating outlook to negative from stable in 1995.
S&P assigns a rating of AAA with a stable rating outlook to Canada's domestic currency debt.

Canada's large debt burden was the key factor preventing the agency from upgrading the country's foreign currency credit rating, said Connell. He noted that with the federal government's debt equal to about 75 percent of gross domestic product, Canada's financial flexibility was limited.
"An upgrade is not likely unless and until significant progress is made on controlling the debt relative to size of the economy," said Connell. "The triple-A ratios still seem a number of years off."

Canada's economy was also susceptible to any slowdown in the U.S. economy or a rise in U.S. interest rates, Connell said. The effects of high unemployment and weak consumer confidence were also a concern, he said.

While Canada appeared on track to begin running budgetary surpluses within the next several years, Connell said the agency was concerned that the federal government might begin to lose some of its resolve to bring down its deficit.
